unit.unitOverview: Analysis means breaking an issue into parts to understand it better. Instead of treating a problem as one big lump, you ask careful questions about the pieces inside it: What exactly is the issue? Why is it happening (causes)? What does it lead to (consequences)? Who is affected, and how do they see it (perspectives)? Then you bring the pieces together into a fair conclusion.

explainers.title: Welcome back to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. In Unit 1 you built your first thinking skill, Research: you learned to ask a good question, gather information from more than one source, and record what you found in your own words. That was the foundation. Now you are ready to build the next skill on top of it.

Remember that this subject grows six skills, and each one supports the others:

This unit is all about the second skill: Analysis. Research told you *what* is happening. Analysis asks the harder and more interesting questions: why is it happening, who sees it differently, and what does it lead to? Once you have gathered good information, analysis is how you make sense of it.

Analysis is a skill you already use, even if you have never called it that. When you work out why your team lost a match, or why one shop is always busier than another, or why two friends remember the same argument differently, you are analysing. In this unit you will learn to do it on purpose, with more care, about real issues in your community and in the wider world.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you have changed your mind.
Collaboration — working well with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so others understand you.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in Ehel Academy's self-paced way, which means three kinds of support work together:

Analysis grows fastest through conversation, because it is about seeing an issue from more than one side. In the old style of this subject, learners were told to 'talk to a partner' or 'discuss as a class'. In our model, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, treat it as a real discussion. Say your idea, then ask the tutor to argue the other side, so you can test whether your thinking really holds up.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. You read, think and complete the activities in your own time. You can slow down on a hard idea, such as telling a fact from an opinion, or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, available 24 hours a day. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were a study partner and a whole class of classmates in one. It will discuss your ideas, challenge your thinking, and give you feedback at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best analysis, ask the questions that matter most, and hear how other learners see the same issue.

explainers.title: Meet Sami, our analyst for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each idea clear, we will follow one Year 7 learner all the way through the unit. His name is Sami, and he is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. In Unit 1 you followed Amal as she researched water; now it is Sami's turn to analyse an issue right outside his door.

On an empty plot near Sami's street, rubbish has slowly been building up. Some families leave their waste there because no truck comes to collect it. Over the dry months the pile has grown, flies have arrived, and after rain the smell drifts down the road. Sami notices that people talk about the pile in very different ways. One neighbour is angry, one shopkeeper shrugs, and a health worker at the clinic worries about mosquitoes. Sami starts to wonder: why is the rubbish piling up, who sees it differently, and what would actually help?

That question becomes Sami's project for this unit. Notice that he is no longer only *finding out* about the rubbish, as he would in Research. He is taking the issue apart: looking for causes, following consequences, and comparing the many perspectives around him. As you meet each new analysis skill, you will see exactly what Sami does with it, and you will do the very same thing with an issue that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the project that runs through the unit
explainers.body:
Just like in Research, this unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. A Challenge is a real issue that matters where you live and also connects to the wider world. You will keep returning to it, lesson after lesson, and each new analysis skill adds another layer to your understanding of it.

You have a choice. You may keep the same Challenge topic you researched in Unit 1 and now analyse it more deeply, which is a great option because you already have information about it. Or you may choose a new issue if something else has caught your attention. Here are some issues that are very real in the Horn of Africa and rich with different perspectives:

The best issue for Analysis is one where people honestly disagree, or see things from different sides. If everyone already agrees on the answer, there is little to analyse. So look for a topic where a market seller, a parent, a student and a leader might each say something different.
bullets: Waste and litter in our streets and empty plots
Clean air, dust and smoke from cooking fuel
Road safety and busy traffic near schools
Fewer fish along the coast (overfishing) near Berbera
Cutting trees for charcoal, and what it does to the land
Clean water for every family in the dry season
Girls staying in school
Protecting endangered wildlife, such as sea turtles on the Berbera coast

explainers.title: What is analysis, really?
explainers.body:
The word analysis simply means breaking something into its parts to understand it better. When you analyse an issue, you stop treating it as one big lump and start asking careful questions about the pieces inside it: What exactly is the problem? Why is it happening? What does it lead to? Who is affected, and how do they see it? A useful way to remember it is this: research gathers the pieces, and analysis works out how the pieces fit together.

Good analysis usually involves several kinds of thinking. In this unit you will practise each one:

That may look like a long list, but every part answers one of three simple questions: *What is going on? Why? And so what?* Keep those three questions in mind and analysis will feel natural.
bullets: Telling the difference between an issue and a perspective.
Seeing an issue from four levels: personal, local, national and global.
Telling a fact from an opinion, and asking what evidence supports a view.
Explaining causes (why something happens) and consequences (what it leads to).
Finding the similarities and differences between sources or viewpoints.
Reading data, such as a bar graph, to spot patterns and support an argument.
Identifying the stakeholders who have an interest in an issue.
Drawing a conclusion and suggesting an action, both supported by evidence.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Telling an issue from a perspective
explainers.body:
Two words sit at the very heart of Analysis, and it is worth getting them clear from the start: issue and perspective.

One helpful test is this: to spot an issue, ask whether a *course of action* might be needed. If people might reasonably say 'someone should do something about this', it is probably an issue. A perspective, on the other hand, is not the problem itself; it is a viewpoint *on* the problem. The same issue can be seen through many different perspectives at once.
bullets: An issue is a problem or an important question that people care about and that might need some action. Waste, poverty, road safety and pollution are all issues.
A perspective is a way of looking at an issue: a certain point of view, shaped by who a person is, where they live, and what they care about.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Seeing an issue at four levels
explainers.body:
A powerful way to analyse any issue is to look at it from four different distances, or levels. The same issue looks different depending on how close you stand to it.

A national perspective thinks about an issue as it relates to one whole country, based on the needs of everyone in it. A global perspective thinks about the issue as it relates to the whole world, and it may come from a country, an organisation, or even one person, as long as its influence spreads beyond any single nation. Strong analysis moves between these levels instead of getting stuck at just one.
bullets: Personal — how the issue affects you and your own family, up close.
Local — how it affects your neighbourhood, town or city.
National — how it affects your whole country.
Global — how it affects the whole world, across many countries.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Telling a fact from an opinion
explainers.body:
When you analyse what people say and write, you must sort two very different things: facts and opinions. Mixing them up is one of the easiest mistakes to make, and one of the most important to avoid.

Both matter in analysis. Facts give you solid ground to stand on. Opinions tell you how people feel and what they value, which is exactly what perspectives are made of. The skill is not to throw opinions away, but to know which is which, so that you never treat a strong opinion as if it were a proven fact.
bullets: A fact is something that can be checked and shown to be true, such as a measurement, a count, or a date.
An opinion is what someone thinks, feels or believes. It cannot simply be looked up, and other people may honestly disagree.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Explaining causes and consequences
explainers.body:
At the centre of analysis is a simple pair of questions: why did this happen, and what does it lead to? The answers are causes and consequences.

Most issues have more than one cause and more than one consequence, and one consequence can become the cause of the next problem, like a chain. Seeing that chain clearly is a big part of analysis. Certain signal words help you spot and explain causes and consequences in what you read and write.
bullets: A cause is the reason why an event or situation is happening or has happened.
A consequence is the result or effect of something that has happened or is happening.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Comparing sources and viewpoints
explainers.body:
Analysis often means placing two things side by side, two sources, or two people's views, and asking: what is the same, and what is different? Finding these similarities and differences helps you see an issue more fully and notice where people agree and where they clash.

When you compare, look for three things: where the two views agree, where they disagree, and what one says that the other leaves out completely. That last one, what is missing, is often the most interesting, because a source usually leaves out the parts that do not suit its perspective.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Reading data to spot patterns
explainers.body:
Not all evidence is words. Some of the strongest evidence is data: numbers, counts and measurements, often shown in a bar graph. A good analyst can read a graph, pull out the important information, and use it to support an argument. Numbers can make a perspective far more convincing than feelings alone.

When you meet a graph, read it in a calm order: first the title (what is it about?), then the labels on each axis (what is being counted, and in what units?), then the bars themselves (which is tallest, which is shortest, and what is the overall pattern?). A double-bar graph is especially useful because it lets you compare two groups side by side, such as boys and girls, or two neighbourhoods, or two seasons.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Identifying the stakeholders
explainers.body:
Every issue has people who care about it, and the special word for them is stakeholders. A stakeholder is anyone with a real interest in an issue, because the issue affects them or they can affect it. Listing the stakeholders is one of the best ways to make sure you have not missed an important perspective.

Two ideas make this skill powerful. First, each group of stakeholders shares knowledge and values that shape how they see the issue, so they tend to have a common perspective. Second, even within one group there can be different perspectives. For example, learners in Grade 7 and learners in Grade 10 are both students, but they may see the same school rule quite differently.

explainers.title: Skill 8: Drawing a supported conclusion
explainers.body:
All of your analysis builds towards one thing: a conclusion you can support with evidence, and often a suggestion for what could be done. A conclusion is not just your first feeling. It is a careful judgement that you reach *after* looking at the causes, the consequences, the data and the different perspectives.

When an issue needs action, analysts often follow a set of problem-solving steps. They help you move calmly from a messy problem to a sensible plan:

explainers.title: Staying fair when you analyse
explainers.body:
Analysis gives you the power to take an issue apart, so it also asks you to be fair. The heart of Global Perspectives is seeing an issue from many sides evenly, before you decide. A fair analyst listens to perspectives they disagree with just as carefully as ones they like.

People's perspectives are shaped by many things: where they live, what work they do, their age, their family, and their culture or beliefs. Noticing this helps you understand a viewpoint instead of just dismissing it.

explainers.title: How analysis links to the other five skills
explainers.body:
Analysis sits in the middle of the six skills, and it connects to every one of them. It takes what research gives you and prepares the way for everything that follows.

So the thinking you practise here is never wasted. Analysis is the bridge between simply knowing about an issue and being able to judge it, discuss it, and act on it wisely.
bullets: Research feeds analysis: you cannot break an issue into causes and perspectives until you have gathered good information.
Evaluation builds on analysis: once you can see the different views, evaluation helps you judge which arguments are actually strongest.
Reflection grows every time you notice how your analysis changed your mind about an issue.
Collaboration improves when you can understand other people's perspectives instead of only your own.
Communication becomes clearer and fairer when it rests on careful analysis rather than on a first reaction.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the analysis cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every analysis skill in this unit. Here is how they fit into one clear cycle you can use for any issue:
bullets: Name the issue clearly, and separate it from the perspectives on it.
Look at the issue at four levels: personal, local, national and global.
Sort the facts from the opinions, and ask what evidence supports each view.
Map the causes and consequences, following the chain.
Compare the different sources and viewpoints for similarities and differences.
Read any data for patterns, and identify the stakeholders.
Draw a conclusion supported by evidence, and suggest a realistic action.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Evaluation. Once you can analyse an issue, breaking it into causes, consequences and perspectives, evaluation teaches you to weigh those perspectives and arguments and judge how strong each one really is. Strong analysis now will make strong evaluation much easier later. Well done for taking your thinking to a new level in Global Perspectives.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is the vehicle, and the skill is the destination.
We will use real issues such as waste, clean air, road safety and fishing, but the point is not to become an expert on rubbish.
The point is to become a clear thinker who can take almost any issue apart, see it from many sides, and reach a fair conclusion.

bigIdeas.title: A quick way to tell them apart
lines: An issue is usually a thing or a problem: waste, water, traffic, poverty.
A perspective is usually a viewpoint about that thing: it is quick and cheap, it is unhealthy, it harms the whole town.
If you can put the words I think or in our view in front of it, you are probably looking at a perspective.

bigIdeas.title: Why the four levels matter
lines: They stop you from thinking an issue is only about you, or only about far-away places.
They help you find perspectives you had not thought of, such as how a national government sees the same problem.
In Global Perspectives, connecting the local and the global, seeing how your street links to the world, is exactly the kind of thinking we are building.

bigIdeas.title: Perspective is not the same as opinion
lines: An opinion is one person's personal thought: I think the air is fine.
A perspective is a wider way of looking at an issue, often shared by a group, such as drivers or parents or health workers.
A strong perspective is supported by evidence and facts, not just by one person's feeling.
So when someone gives a view, a good analyst asks: what fact or evidence backs this up?

bigIdeas.title: Signal words for cause and consequence
lines: Words that signal a cause: because, since, due to, as a result of, the reason is, caused by.
Words that signal a consequence: so, therefore, as a result, this means that, consequently, this leads to.
When you read a source, underline these words. They point straight to the reasons and the effects.

bigIdeas.title: Graphs as evidence
lines: A bar graph is a clear way to present research findings, and a strong way to support an argument.
A double-bar graph lets you compare two groups, such as two seasons or two age groups.
Always read the title and labels first, or the bars can fool you.
Ask what the pattern is, and what might have caused it.

bigIdeas.title: Basic problem-solving steps
lines: 1. Identify the issue — name the real problem.
2. Explain the issue — describe its causes and consequences.
3. Search for and organise information — gather what different sources and perspectives say.
4. Identify the resources needed — work out what a solution would require.
5. Form a plan — choose a realistic course of action.
6. Evaluate the course of action — ask whether it would really help.

A course of action is the step you suggest to help with an issue. To be worth suggesting, it must be realistic and it must fit the issue: a local issue usually needs a local action. A good course of action also has a clear outcome, something people can see or do, such as a poster to raise awareness, a letter to persuade a leader, or an event to bring people together.

bigIdeas.title: Different lives, different perspectives
lines: Imagine a school deciding when to serve its main meal during a month of fasting.
A family that fasts for Ramadan and a family that fasts during Lent might each have a clear perspective on the timing.
Neither is simply right or wrong; each comes from that family's way of life.
A fair analyst hears both evenly and looks for a solution that respects everyone.

bigIdeas.title: Watch out for bias
lines: Bias is when a source or a person leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.
A view is not automatically wrong because it has a side, but you should notice the side it takes.
Balance a strong view from one group by finding an equally strong view from another.
Being fair does not mean having no opinion. It means forming your opinion only after hearing many sides.

bigIdeas.title: The three questions of analysis
lines: Whenever you feel stuck, come back to these three simple questions.
What is going on? Name the issue clearly.
Why? Find the causes and the different perspectives.
So what? Follow the consequences and reach a conclusion.
Every tool in this file helps you answer one of these three questions.

bigIdeas.title: Remember
lines: Facts give you solid ground; opinions tell you how people feel.
You need both, but you must always know which is which.
A strong perspective is an opinion backed by evidence.

bigIdeas.title: Signal words to look for
lines: Cause words: because, since, due to, as a result of, the reason is, caused by.
Consequence words: so, therefore, as a result, this means that, consequently, this leads to.
Underline these in any source; they point straight to causes and effects.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Choose one real issue to analyse across this whole unit. This is your Challenge.
You may keep the topic you researched in Unit 1, or pick a new issue where people disagree.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something you genuinely care about.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a good questionnaire question
lines: It is clear about what it is asking.
It relates to your issue and the perspective you want to understand.
Yes or No questions are quick to answer and easy to turn into a graph.
It is not leading. A leading question pushes people toward one answer, such as: Do you agree the plot is disgusting?

models.title: Analysis happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine the water tap in your home suddenly runs dry one morning.
Research would ask: is it dry in the whole street, or only our house?
Analysis goes further. It asks why: perhaps a pipe has burst, or the dry season has emptied the tank, or many new homes now share the same supply.
It asks about consequences: the family cannot cook or wash, and someone must walk to buy water.
It asks about perspectives: a neighbour, the water seller and the council would each explain the shortage differently.
Working all of that out, not just noticing the dry tap, is analysis. You already do it.

So analysis is not a strange school-only activity. It is the careful thinking you use whenever you want to understand *why* something is the way it is. In this unit you will simply do it more deliberately, and about issues that matter to your community.

models.title: Sami's example: one issue, many perspectives
lines: The issue: rubbish is piling up on the empty plot, and it may need action.
One perspective comes from a neighbour beside the plot: the smell and flies are making her home unpleasant and unhealthy.
Another comes from a market seller: dumping there is quick and free, and he has no time to carry waste further.
Another comes from the health worker at the clinic: standing water in the rubbish breeds mosquitoes, which spread disease.
Notice there is one issue but three perspectives. None of them is the issue itself; each is a way of seeing it.

models.title: Sami's example: rubbish at four levels
lines: Personal: the smell reaches Sami's home, and his little sister cannot play safely near the plot.
Local: across the neighbourhood, blocked drains flood after rain, and the clinic sees more sickness.
National: many towns across the country struggle to collect and manage waste as cities grow.
Global: waste and burning rubbish add to pollution and climate change that affect every country.
It is the same rubbish, seen at four distances. Each level adds something the others miss.

You do not always need all four levels for every issue, but trying each one stops you from thinking too narrowly. A learner who only ever sees the personal level misses the bigger picture, and a learner who only talks about the global level forgets the real people next door.

models.title: Layla's example: sorting facts from opinions
lines: Layla is analysing the dusty, smoky air near a busy junction in her area.
Fact: on three mornings she counted more than forty vehicles passing in ten minutes. This can be checked.
Fact: the clinic recorded more chest complaints during the dry, dusty months. This is a record.
Opinion: a driver says the air is fine and people worry too much. This is a belief, not proof.
Opinion: a parent says the council does not care about children. This is a feeling, not a checked fact.
Layla keeps all four, but labels each one, so she does not confuse how people feel with what is true.

models.title: Rami's example: a dangerous road in Mogadishu
lines: Rami is analysing why a road near his school in Mogadishu feels dangerous.
Causes: there is no safe crossing, cars drive fast, and the road is crowded at the start and end of school.
Consequences: as a result, there are frequent near-misses, parents are frightened, and some younger children are kept at home on busy days.
Notice the chain: fast cars and no crossing lead to near-misses, which lead to frightened parents, which lead to children missing school.

models.title: Sami's example: the causes and consequences of the rubbish
lines: Causes: no collection truck comes, the neighbourhood is growing, and dumping on the plot is quick and free.
Consequences: therefore the pile grows, flies and mosquitoes arrive, drains block, and after rain the streets flood and smell.
One consequence, blocked drains, becomes the cause of the next problem, flooding. Sami maps the whole chain.

models.title: Sami's example: two views on the rubbish plot
lines: View one, from a market seller: the plot is a handy place to dump waste, it costs nothing, and it is not really his problem.
View two, from a neighbour beside the plot: the waste is a health danger and the town should organise a proper collection.
Similarity: both agree that a lot of rubbish ends up on the plot.
Difference: they disagree about whose problem it is and whether action is needed.
What is missing: the seller says nothing about health, and the neighbour says nothing about why collection has stopped. Each leaves out what does not suit them.

Comparing is not about deciding at once who is right. It is about mapping the ground carefully first. Once you can see clearly where views meet and part, you are in a much stronger position to reach a fair conclusion later.

models.title: Nadia's example: a double-bar graph of drinks
lines: Nadia is analysing what students drink at school. For five days she counts how many bring a sugary drink and how many bring water.
She draws a double-bar graph: for each day, one bar for sugary drinks and one for water, so the two can be compared.
The pattern is clear at a glance: sugary drinks are higher on most days.
But there is a second pattern. On the day after a health talk, both bars for sugary drinks drop. The talk may be a cause of the change.
The graph does not just show numbers. It supports Nadia's argument that lessons about health can change what students choose.

Before you look closely at a graph, it is a good habit to make a prediction: a statement of what you think the data will show. Then you check the graph against your prediction. Whether you were right or wrong, you learn something, and comparing your guess to the real pattern is analysis in action.

models.title: Sami's example: who are the stakeholders?
lines: Families near the plot, who live with the smell and flies every day.
Market sellers, who use the plot because it is quick and free.
The health worker at the clinic, who sees the sickness the waste can cause.
The town council, who would have to pay for and organise a collection.
Children, who play near the plot and cannot always be kept away.
Even within one group there are differences: an older neighbour may want to act, while a busy young parent may feel too tired to join in.

Once you can name the stakeholders, you can ask the most useful analysis question of all: for each of these groups, how would they finish the sentence 'the most important thing about this issue is...'? Their answers are the perspectives you need.

models.title: Sami's example: from analysis to a conclusion
lines: Sami gathers his analysis: the cause is no collection, the consequences are flies, blocked drains and sickness, and the stakeholders disagree about whose job it is.
His survey of twenty neighbours shows that most would join a shared clean-up if someone organised it.

His conclusion, supported by that evidence: the rubbish is a shared local problem, and the strongest first step is a neighbourhood collection day plus a letter to the council asking for a regular truck.
Notice the conclusion rests on evidence, not just on Sami feeling annoyed. That is what makes it strong.

You will not solve a whole issue in one unit, and that is fine. The skill is to reach a fair, evidence-based conclusion and suggest a sensible next step. That honest, careful judgement is the true goal of Analysis.

models.title: Sami's whole journey, from a rubbish pile to a plan
lines: Skill 1: He separated the issue, the growing waste, from the many perspectives on it.
Skill 2: He saw the rubbish at four levels, from the smell at home to global pollution.
Skill 3: He sorted facts, such as counts of the flies and floods, from opinions about whose fault it was.
Skill 4: He mapped the causes, no collection, and the consequences, sickness and flooding.
Skill 5: He compared the market seller's view with the neighbour's view.
Skills 6 and 7: He used his survey data and listed every stakeholder.
Skill 8: He reached an evidence-based conclusion and suggested a clean-up day plus a letter to the council.

By following this cycle, Sami turned a confusing, smelly problem into clear thinking and a sensible plan. In the Activities file, you will run the same cycle on your own Challenge issue, one step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you the whole way.

models.title: A model, in case you get stuck: clean air
lines: Personal: the dust makes my younger brother cough at home.
Local: smoke and dust hang over the busiest streets of our town.
National: many growing cities in our country face the same dusty, smoky air.
Global: air pollution and burning fuel add to climate change everywhere.

models.title: A model: fact or opinion
lines: Statement: three drains overflowed after the storm last month. This is a fact, because it can be checked.
Statement: the council is simply lazy. This is an opinion, because it is a belief others might dispute.
A fact that could test that opinion: how many collection days the council actually managed last month.

models.title: A model: the rubbish plot
lines: Issue in the centre: rubbish piles up on the empty plot.
Causes: because no truck collects it; because the area is growing; because dumping there is free.
Consequences: as a result, flies and mosquitoes spread; drains block; after rain the street floods.
Arrow: blocked drains (a consequence) become the cause of flooding (a new problem).

When your map is done, turn it into a short spoken commentary: two or three sentences that name the situation, its main cause, and its main consequence. Practising this out loud helps you explain your issue clearly to someone else, which you will need when you draw your conclusion later.

models.title: A model: two views on a busy road
lines: Viewpoint one, Malik, a boda-boda rider: the road is how he earns his living, so slowing down means fewer trips and less money.
Viewpoint two, Amara, a parent: the fast motorbikes frighten her young children on their way to school.
Similarity: both use the same road every day, and both want to reach places quickly.
Difference: they disagree about whether the speed is a danger or a need.
Missing: Malik says nothing about children's safety, and Amara says nothing about how riders earn a living.

models.title: A model: stakeholders for the rubbish plot
lines: Families beside the plot: they care about health and the smell.
Market sellers: they care about a quick, free place to dump waste.
The clinic health worker: cares about disease from mosquitoes.
The town council: cares about the cost of collection.
Children: they play nearby and are hard to keep away.

models.title: A model: Sami's conclusion and action
lines: Evidence: no truck collects the waste; the clinic reports more sickness; most neighbours would join a clean-up.
Conclusion: the rubbish is a shared local problem that the neighbourhood and council must tackle together.
Course of action: organise a neighbourhood collection day and write a letter to the council asking for a regular truck.
How the evidence supports it: because most neighbours would help, a shared day is realistic; because sickness is rising, action is urgent.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 2 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Analysis.
Ask it: In one or two sentences, what is the difference between researching an issue and analysing it?
Then tell the tutor one issue in your area that you would like to understand better, and why it matters to you.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think analysis means.
Ask it: How is analysis different from research?

speakingPrompts.title: A human touch
lines: Ask a family member about an issue in your area that they feel strongly about.

toolkit.title: The analysis cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your issue, good analysis follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: Name the issue: say clearly what the problem is, apart from any one view of it.
Zoom in and out: look at it at the personal, local, national and global levels.
Sort fact from opinion: and ask what evidence supports each view.
Find causes and consequences: ask why it happens and what it leads to.
Compare viewpoints: look for similarities, differences, and what is missing.
Read the data and list the stakeholders: find patterns and the people who care.
Conclude and suggest action: reach an evidence-based judgement and a realistic step.

toolkit.title: The Analysis skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Analysis means breaking an issue into parts to understand it better. Instead of treating a problem as one big lump, you ask careful questions about the pieces inside it: What exactly is the issue? Why is it happening (causes)? What does it lead to (consequences)? Who is affected, and how do they see it (perspectives)? Then you bring the pieces together into a fair conclusion.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always look for more than one perspective, because every issue looks different depending on who is standing where. Second, always ask for the evidence behind a view, so you never mistake a strong opinion for a proven fact. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 7 Analysis objectives
toolkit.intro: Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong analysis looks like at this stage. Here are the official Analysis objectives, restated simply. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

rows: Identify ideas and evidence from different perspectives within different sources on a given topic.
Find the different points of view inside the sources you read, and the evidence behind each one.
Explain how graphical or numerical data supports an argument.
Read a graph or numbers, spot the pattern, and use it to back up a point.
Explain causes of a local or global issue and the consequences on others.
Say why an issue happens and what effects it has on people.
Suggest and justify different actions to make a positive difference to a national or global issue.
Suggest a realistic action to help, and give good reasons for it.

toolkit.title: Issue and perspective
toolkit.intro: Quick test: if you might say 'someone should do something about this', it is an issue. If you can put 'I think' or 'in our view' in front of it, it is a perspective.

rows: A problem or important question that people care about and that may need action.
A way of looking at an issue, shaped by who someone is and where they live.
It is unhealthy; it is quick and cheap; it harms the whole town.

toolkit.title: Template: An issue at four levels
toolkit.intro: Copy this table for your issue. Fill in how the issue looks at each level. It stops you from thinking too narrowly.

rows: How does it affect me and my family?
How does it affect my neighbourhood or town?
How does it affect my whole country?
How does it connect to the whole world?

toolkit.title: Template: Cause and consequence map
toolkit.intro: Put your issue in the middle row. List the causes (why it happens) and the consequences (what it leads to). Watch for a consequence that becomes the cause of a new problem.

rows: Chain (a consequence that causes a new problem)

toolkit.title: Template: Compare two sources or viewpoints
toolkit.intro: Use this grid to compare any two sources or views. The 'what is missing' row is often the most revealing.

toolkit.title: Template: Stakeholder list
toolkit.intro: List every group with an interest in your issue, and what each one cares about most. Remember that perspectives can differ even inside one group.

toolkit.title: The problem-solving steps
toolkit.intro:
When an issue needs action, work through these steps in order to move from a messy problem to a sensible plan.

A good course of action is realistic, fits the size of the issue (a local issue needs a local action), and has a clear outcome, such as a poster, a letter, or an event.
items: Identify the issue — name the real problem.
Explain the issue — describe its causes and consequences.
Search for and organise information — gather what different sources and perspectives say.
Identify the resources needed — work out what a solution would require.
Form a plan — choose a realistic course of action.
Evaluate the course of action — ask whether it would really help.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for analysis
toolkit.intro: Use these to write clear analysis. Mix and match them as you need.

toolkit.title: For causes and consequences:
items: This happens because ...
One cause of this is ...
As a result of this, ...
This leads to ... which then causes ...

toolkit.title: For perspectives and comparing:
items: From a personal / local / national / global perspective, ...
One group sees this as ... while another sees it as ...
Both views agree that ... but they differ on ...
This source leaves out ...

toolkit.title: For conclusions and actions:
items: The evidence suggests that ...
Taking all the perspectives together, I conclude that ...
One realistic action would be ... because ...
This action fits the issue because ...

checklists.title: Checklist: Is it a fact or an opinion?
checklists.intro: Ask these questions about any statement before you rely on it.
items: Can it be checked or measured? If yes, it is probably a fact.
Could sensible people disagree with it? If yes, it is probably an opinion.
Does it use feeling words like best, worst, terrible or wonderful? Those often signal an opinion.
If it is an opinion, ask: what fact or evidence supports it?

checklists.title: Checklist: Reading a graph
checklists.intro: Read a graph in this order so it cannot fool you. A bar graph presents findings clearly and supports an argument. A double-bar graph compares two groups side by side, such as two seasons, two neighbourhoods, or boys and girls.
items: Read the title: what is the graph about?
Read the labels on each axis: what is counted, and in what units?
Look at the bars: which is tallest, which is shortest?
Name the pattern: what is the overall story?
Ask why: what might have caused the pattern?

challenge.intro: Look back at the issue list in the Lesson file (waste, clean air, road safety, overfishing, charcoal and trees, clean water, girls in school, endangered wildlife). Choose one that matters where you live, or continue with your Unit 1 topic. The best issue for analysis is one where different people would honestly say different things.
topics: Write your chosen issue in one sentence: 'The issue I am analysing is ...'.
Write one reason it matters to you personally.
Name two people or groups who might see this issue very differently from each other.
checkpoints: I was surprised to discover that ...

activities.title: Issue or perspective?
activities.label: Activity 2: Issue or perspective?
activities.intro:
Remember the difference: an issue is a problem that might need action, and a perspective is a way of looking at an issue. Sort the eight words below into two columns: 'Issue' and 'Perspective (level)'.

Write each word under the right heading. Then, in one sentence of your own, explain the difference between an issue and a perspective. If a word feels like it could go in either column, that is worth noticing: some words, like Cultural or Global, are really the *level* from which you view an issue, not the issue itself.
steps: Pollution
Personal
Poverty
National
Homelessness
Local
Crime
Global

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two columns to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain any word you were unsure about, in a simple way.
Then ask the tutor: for my own Challenge issue, what are two perspective levels I could use?

activities.title: Your issue at four levels
activities.label: Activity 3: Your issue at four levels
activities.intro: Analyse your Challenge issue from four distances. For each level, write one or two sentences about how the issue looks from there. Do not worry if the global level is harder; give it your best try.
steps: Personal: how does this issue affect you and your family?
Local: how does it affect your neighbourhood or town?
National: how does it affect your whole country?
Global: how does it connect to the wider world?

boxes.title: A model, in case you get stuck: clean air
lines: Personal: the dust makes my younger brother cough at home.
Local: smoke and dust hang over the busiest streets of our town.
National: many growing cities in our country face the same dusty, smoky air.
Global: air pollution and burning fuel add to climate change everywhere.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four levels to your AI tutor.
Ask it which level is strongest and which needs more detail.
Ask the tutor to help you improve the level you found hardest to write.

activities.title: Fact or opinion?
activities.label: Activity 4: Fact or opinion?
activities.intro:
A good analyst never mixes up a fact (which can be checked) with an opinion (which someone believes). Read the six statements below and label each one F for fact or O for opinion.

Write F or O next to each letter. Then, for one statement you marked O, write one fact that could support or challenge that opinion.
steps: A. After heavy rain, the drain near the market overflowed three times last year.
B. The council simply does not care about our neighbourhood.
C. More than thirty motorbikes passed the school gate in ten minutes.
D. Plastic bags are the worst thing that has ever happened to our town.
E. The clinic recorded more chest complaints during the dusty months.
F. Everyone knows that fishing should just be banned.

boxes.title: A model: fact or opinion
lines: Statement: three drains overflowed after the storm last month. This is a fact, because it can be checked.
Statement: the council is simply lazy. This is an opinion, because it is a belief others might dispute.
A fact that could test that opinion: how many collection days the council actually managed last month.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six labels to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain any that you found tricky, especially ones that sound like facts but are really opinions.
Then ask the tutor to help you write two statements about my own issue: one clear fact and one clear opinion.

activities.title: Map the causes and consequences
activities.label: Activity 5: Map the causes and consequences
activities.intro: Put your issue in the middle. On one side, list what causes it (the reasons why). On the other side, list its consequences (what it leads to). Use the signal words to help you: because and due to point to causes; so and as a result point to consequences.
steps: Write your issue in the centre of a page.
On the left, write two or three causes. Start each with 'This happens because ...'.
On the right, write two or three consequences. Start each with 'As a result, ...'.
Draw an arrow from any consequence that then becomes the cause of a new problem.

boxes.title: A model: the rubbish plot
lines: Issue in the centre: rubbish piles up on the empty plot.
Causes: because no truck collects it; because the area is growing; because dumping there is free.
Consequences: as a result, flies and mosquitoes spread; drains block; after rain the street floods.
Arrow: blocked drains (a consequence) become the cause of flooding (a new problem).

When your map is done, turn it into a short spoken commentary: two or three sentences that name the situation, its main cause, and its main consequence. Practising this out loud helps you explain your issue clearly to someone else, which you will need when you draw your conclusion later.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your cause-and-consequence map to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether any cause or consequence is missing.
Ask the tutor to help you find one place where a consequence becomes the cause of the next problem.

boxes.title: A real-world step
lines: Ask a family member or neighbour what they think causes your issue.
Compare their answer with your map. Did they name a cause you had missed?
Bring the difference to your next teacher session.

activities.title: Compare two viewpoints
activities.label: Activity 6: Compare two viewpoints
activities.intro:
Choose two people or groups who see your issue differently, for example a market seller and a neighbour, or a driver and a parent. Write a short description of each viewpoint. Then compare them using the grid idea below.

The 'missing' question is the most interesting. What a viewpoint leaves out often tells you what that group does not want to think about.
steps: Write viewpoint one in two or three sentences.
Write viewpoint two in two or three sentences.
Similarity: what do both viewpoints agree on?
Difference: where do they clash?
Missing: what does each viewpoint leave out?

boxes.title: A model: two views on a busy road
lines: Viewpoint one, Malik, a boda-boda rider: the road is how he earns his living, so slowing down means fewer trips and less money.
Viewpoint two, Amara, a parent: the fast motorbikes frighten her young children on their way to school.
Similarity: both use the same road every day, and both want to reach places quickly.
Difference: they disagree about whether the speed is a danger or a need.
Missing: Malik says nothing about children's safety, and Amara says nothing about how riders earn a living.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your two viewpoints to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you name one similarity, one difference, and one thing each side leaves out.
Then ask the tutor: what does the missing part reveal about each group's perspective?

activities.title: Read the data
activities.label: Activity 7: Read the data
activities.intro:
Data can make an argument strong. Below is a small set of numbers from an imaginary count. Read it carefully, then answer the questions. Nadia counted, on five school days, how many students in her class brought a sugary drink and how many brought water.

Now analyse the data:

Before you check with your tutor, make a prediction: what do you think would happen to the numbers if the health talk was repeated every week?
steps: On which day were the fewest sugary drinks brought?
What pattern do you notice across the week?
What might have caused the change on Wednesday and Thursday?
Write one sentence using this data to support an argument.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers and your prediction to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you spotted the main pattern and named a sensible cause.
Ask the tutor how you could show this data as a double-bar graph, and what the two bars would be.

activities.title: Map your stakeholders
activities.label: Activity 8: Map your stakeholders
activities.intro: A stakeholder is anyone with a real interest in your issue. Brainstorm as many as you can. The more stakeholders you find, the more perspectives you will be able to analyse.
steps: Write your issue in the centre of a page.
Around it, write every stakeholder group you can think of, at least five.
For each group, write one word or phrase for what they care about most.
Circle one group whose perspective is very different from your own.

boxes.title: A model: stakeholders for the rubbish plot
lines: Families beside the plot: they care about health and the smell.
Market sellers: they care about a quick, free place to dump waste.
The clinic health worker: cares about disease from mosquitoes.
The town council: cares about the cost of collection.
Children: they play nearby and are hard to keep away.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your stakeholder map to your AI tutor.
Ask it to suggest one or two stakeholder groups you may have missed.
Then pick one group and ask the tutor to help you imagine different perspectives inside that single group.

activities.title: Design a questionnaire to find a new perspective
activities.label: Activity 9: Design a questionnaire to find a new perspective
activities.intro: To understand an issue fully, you must actively search for a perspective that is different from your own. A short questionnaire is a good way to do this. Design one to gain the perspective of one stakeholder group you chose in Activity 8.
steps: Decide which stakeholder group you will ask.
Write six clear questions. Include some with a simple Yes or No answer, because these are easy to count and to show on a graph.
Check each question: is it clear, is it fair, and does it avoid pushing people toward one answer?
Rewrite any question that is unclear or leading.

boxes.title: What makes a good questionnaire question
lines: It is clear about what it is asking.
It relates to your issue and the perspective you want to understand.
Yes or No questions are quick to answer and easy to turn into a graph.
It is not leading. A leading question pushes people toward one answer, such as: Do you agree the plot is disgusting?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are any of my questions leading or unclear, and how would you fix them?
Ask the tutor whether my questions will really reveal this group's perspective.

boxes.title: A real-world step
lines: With a trusted adult's help, ask your questionnaire to a few people from that stakeholder group.
Count the answers to your Yes or No questions.
Bring your findings to your next teacher session and compare them with what you expected.

activities.title: Draw a conclusion and suggest an action
activities.label: Activity 10: Draw a conclusion and suggest an action
activities.intro: Now bring your whole analysis together. A strong conclusion is built on evidence, the causes, consequences, data and perspectives you have gathered, not just on how you feel. This is the moment where all the earlier activities pay off, so keep your cause map, your comparison grid and your stakeholder list beside you.
steps: Write down the three strongest pieces of evidence from your analysis so far.
Write one conclusion that those pieces of evidence support.
Suggest one realistic course of action that fits your issue, with a clear outcome (a poster, a letter, an event, a shared day).
Write one sentence explaining how your evidence supports your suggested action.

boxes.title: A model: Sami's conclusion and action
lines: Evidence: no truck collects the waste; the clinic reports more sickness; most neighbours would join a clean-up.
Conclusion: the rubbish is a shared local problem that the neighbourhood and council must tackle together.
Course of action: organise a neighbourhood collection day and write a letter to the council asking for a regular truck.
How the evidence supports it: because most neighbours would help, a shared day is realistic; because sickness is rising, action is urgent.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your evidence, conclusion and course of action to your AI tutor.
Ask it: is my conclusion really supported by my evidence, or am I jumping ahead?
Ask the tutor whether my course of action is realistic and fits the size of my issue.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Try every question before you look at the answer key, and give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'analysis' mean?
practice.answer: Analysis means breaking an issue into parts to understand it, by asking why it happens, what it leads to, and how different people see it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: What is the difference between an issue and a perspective?
practice.answer: An issue is a problem that may need action; a perspective is a way of looking at that issue.

practice.prompt: Name the four levels you can use to look at an issue.
practice.answer: Personal, local, national and global.

practice.prompt: True or false: 'The council does not care about us' is a fact.
practice.answer: False. It is an opinion, because it is a belief that others might dispute, not something you can simply check.

practice.prompt: A ______ is the reason why something happens; a ______ is the result of something happening.
practice.answer: A cause is the reason why something happens; a consequence is the result.

practice.prompt: Give one signal word that points to a cause, and one that points to a consequence.
practice.answer: Cause word: any of because, since, due to, as a result of. Consequence word: any of so, therefore, as a result, consequently.

practice.prompt: What is a stakeholder?
practice.answer: A stakeholder is anyone with a real interest in an issue because it affects them or they can affect it.

practice.prompt: True or false: everyone in the same stakeholder group always has exactly the same perspective.
practice.answer: False. Even within one group there can be different perspectives.

practice.prompt: Which kind of graph lets you compare two groups side by side?
practice.answer: A double-bar graph.

practice.prompt: Before you study a graph closely, it is a good habit to make a ______ about what it will show.
practice.answer: A prediction.

practice.prompt: When you compare two viewpoints, name the three things you should look for.
practice.answer: What they agree on (similarity), where they disagree (difference), and what each one leaves out (missing).

practice.prompt: A national perspective is about one whole ______; a global perspective is about the whole ______.
practice.answer: One whole country; the whole world.

practice.prompt: A realistic step suggested to help with an issue is called a ______ of action.
practice.answer: A course of action.

practice.prompt: Why should a conclusion be supported by evidence and not just by your feelings?
practice.answer: Because a conclusion based only on feelings can be unfair or wrong; evidence makes it trustworthy and lets others check it.

practice.prompt: Put these problem-solving steps in order: (A) form a plan, (B) identify the issue, (C) explain the issue, (D) search for and organise information.
practice.answer: Correct order: B, C, D, A.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each analysis word (1 to 8) to the correct meaning (A to H). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Issue
options: A. The result or effect of something that has happened.
B. A way of looking at an issue, a point of view.
C. Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
D. A realistic step suggested to help with an issue.
E. A problem or important question that people care about.
F. Anyone with a real interest in an issue because it affects them.
G. The reason why something happens.
H. What someone thinks or believes, which others may dispute.
practice.answer: E — A problem or important question that people care about.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Perspective
practice.answer: B — A way of looking at an issue, a point of view.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Cause
practice.answer: G — The reason why something happens.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Consequence
practice.answer: A — The result or effect of something that has happened.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Fact
practice.answer: C — Something that can be checked and shown to be true.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Opinion
practice.answer: H — What someone thinks or believes, which others may dispute.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Stakeholder
practice.answer: F — Anyone with a real interest in an issue because it affects them.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Course of action
practice.answer: D — A realistic step suggested to help with an issue.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Rami says the road by his school is dangerous because cars drive fast and there is no crossing. Which part of his sentence is the cause, and which is the consequence?
practice.answer: Cause: cars drive fast and there is no crossing. Consequence: the road is dangerous.

practice.prompt: A market seller says dumping on the plot is fine, while a neighbour says it is a health danger. What is the issue, and what are the two perspectives?
practice.answer: The issue is the rubbish dumped on the plot. The two perspectives are the seller's (it is quick and free) and the neighbour's (it is a health danger).

practice.prompt: Layla read: 'The clinic recorded more coughs in the dusty months.' Is this a fact or an opinion, and how could she check it?
practice.answer: It is a fact, because it is a record that can be checked. Layla could ask the clinic for its records or compare months.

practice.prompt: Zara is analysing fewer fish along the coast. Name one personal-level effect and one global-level connection.
practice.answer: Personal-level effect: her family can catch or afford fewer fish. Global connection: overfishing is a worldwide problem affecting oceans everywhere.

practice.prompt: Sami found that most neighbours would join a clean-up. How could he show this finding as evidence to the council?
practice.answer: He could show the survey result as a number or a simple bar graph, so the council sees that most neighbours would help.

practice.prompt: Nadia's graph shows sugary drinks dropping the day after a health talk. Is the health talk a cause or a consequence of the drop?
practice.answer: A cause. The health talk came first and led to the drop, so it is the reason for the change, not its result.

practice.prompt: Two neighbours disagree about the rubbish plot. Is their disagreement an issue or two perspectives on an issue? Explain.
practice.answer: Two perspectives on one issue. The issue is the rubbish on the plot; the disagreement is two different ways of viewing that same issue.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own pace ...
Working with my AI tutor, my discussion partner ...
Working with my teacher in live sessions ...
Asking a family member or neighbour for their perspective ...
Mapping my ideas, such as causes, levels and stakeholders, on paper ...

vocabulary.meaning: Breaking an issue into parts to understand it, by asking why, what it leads to, and how people see it.
A problem or important question that people care about and that may need action.
A way of looking at an issue, shaped by who someone is and where they live.
How an issue looks to you and your own family, up close.
How an issue affects your neighbourhood or town.
How an issue relates to one whole country and its people.
How an issue relates to the whole world, across many countries.
Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
What someone thinks or believes, which others may dispute.
Facts or information that support an idea or a view.
The reason why an event or situation happens or has happened.
The result or effect of something that has happened or is happening.
A word that points to a cause or a consequence, such as because or therefore.
Anyone with a real interest in an issue because it affects them or they can affect it.
A single point of view held by a person or group.
Something that two sources or views have in common.
A way in which two sources or views are not the same.
When a source or person leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.
Information in the form of numbers, counts or measurements.
A chart that shows amounts as bars, useful for presenting findings.
A bar graph that compares two groups side by side.
A repeated or overall shape in data that tells you something.
A statement of what you think will happen or what the data will show.
A careful judgement reached after weighing the evidence and perspectives.
A realistic step suggested to help with an issue, with a clear outcome.
An ordered set of steps for moving from a problem to a sensible plan.
Actually useful for understanding your particular issue.
A short spoken or written explanation of a situation, its cause and its consequence.
Anywhere your information comes from: a person, book, website, graph or video.
To do with one whole country and the people in it.
To do with the whole world, across many countries.

mistakes: Describing only your own perspective and forgetting the others.
Treating a strong opinion as if it were a proven fact.
Naming a cause but forgetting the consequences, or the other way round.
Getting stuck at one level, such as only the personal or only the global.
Comparing two views but never asking what each one leaves out.
Reading only the bars of a graph without checking the title and labels.
Jumping to a conclusion before you have looked at the evidence.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'analysis' mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Analysis means breaking an issue into parts to understand it, by asking why it happens, what it leads to, and how different people see it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an issue and a perspective?
questions.modelAnswer: An issue is a problem that may need action; a perspective is a way of looking at that issue.

questions.prompt: Name the four levels you can use to look at an issue.
True or false: 'The council does not care about us' is a fact.
questions.modelAnswer: False. It is an opinion, because it is a belief that others might dispute, not something you can simply check.

questions.prompt: A ______ is the reason why something happens; a ______ is the result of something happening.
questions.modelAnswer: A cause is the reason why something happens; a consequence is the result.

questions.prompt: Give one signal word that points to a cause, and one that points to a consequence.
questions.modelAnswer: Cause word: any of because, since, due to, as a result of. Consequence word: any of so, therefore, as a result, consequently.
A stakeholder is anyone with a real interest in an issue because it affects them or they can affect it.

questions.prompt: True or false: everyone in the same stakeholder group always has exactly the same perspective.
questions.modelAnswer: False. Even within one group there can be different perspectives.

questions.prompt: Which kind of graph lets you compare two groups side by side?
Before you study a graph closely, it is a good habit to make a ______ about what it will show.
When you compare two viewpoints, name the three things you should look for.
questions.modelAnswer: What they agree on (similarity), where they disagree (difference), and what each one leaves out (missing).

questions.prompt: A national perspective is about one whole ______; a global perspective is about the whole ______.
questions.modelAnswer: One whole country; the whole world.

selfAssessment.statement: I can tell the difference between an issue and a perspective.
I can look at an issue from personal, local, national and global levels.
I can tell a fact from an opinion, and ask what evidence supports a view.
I can explain the causes of an issue and its consequences on others.
I can find similarities and differences between two sources or viewpoints.
I can read a graph and explain how the data supports an argument.
I can identify the stakeholders who have an interest in an issue.
I can suggest and justify a realistic action for a local or global issue.
I can draw a conclusion that is supported by evidence.
